Rabbi Yehiel Michel Halevi Epstein: A Comprehensive Study of the Author of the "Arukh HaShulhan"

The text surveys the extensive œuvre of Rabbi Yehiel Michel Halevi Epstein, author of the "Arukh HaShulhan" ("Set Table"), and presents him as an architect of living halakhah connected to modern reality. The article emphasizes his unique methodology, which aspires to encompass all of the Torah while giving decisive weight to Jewish custom and employing clear and accessible language. Alongside a comparative analysis between his approach to practical adjudication and the rulings of the "Mishnah Berurah" ("Clear Teaching"), the text reveals the decisor's boldness in confronting social changes, general education, and anticipation of redemption. Ultimately, the source describes how his work bridges classical Lithuanian tradition and the challenges of the time, while ensuring the relevance of his rulings for future generations as well.

The Torah Thought, Halakhic Activity, and Social Philosophy of Rabbi Yehiel Michel Halevi Epstein: A Comprehensive Study of the Author of the "Arukh HaShulhan"

The history of halakhic adjudication in the modern era is marked by a series of major codifications, yet few compositions have succeeded in encompassing the totality of Jewish life with the same level of thoroughness, clarity, and boldness as the "Arukh HaShulhan." Its author, Rabbi Yehiel Michel Halevi Epstein, operated during a period of tremendous transformation in Eastern European Jewry, and his work reflects a unique attempt to bridge the traditional halakhic world and the changing reality of the nineteenth and early twentieth centuries.[1, 2] Rabbi Epstein's stature is not limited to his role as a halakhic decisor; he was a dominant communal rabbi, a broad-minded thinker, and a spiritual leader who ordained an entire generation of Torah luminaries who influenced the shaping of Judaism in subsequent generations, among them Rabbi Abraham Isaac Kook and Rabbi Isser Zalman Meltzer.[1, 2]

Historical Background and Biography: The Emergence of a Genius Amid the Transformations of the Era

Rabbi Yehiel Michel Halevi Epstein was born in Bobruisk in the Russian Empire (present-day Belarus) on January 24, 1829, the 20th of Shevat 5589.[1, 2] This period was characterized by profound internal tension within Jewish society, between conservatism and the Haskalah movement that was gaining momentum, alongside external pressures from the Tsarist government. His family, the Epstein family, was considered one of the most distinguished and honored families in Lithuanian Jewry. According to family traditions, the family is a descendant of the Sephardic Benveniste family and of Rabbi Aharon HaLevi.[2] The account of the family's name change from "Benveniste" to "Epstein" after the expulsion from Spain, as an expression of gratitude to the people of the town of Eppstein in Germany who received them, attests to a deep historical consciousness and a sense of commitment to tradition and community.[2] His father, Rabbi Aharon Yitzhak HaLevi, was engaged in commerce, a fact that contributed to the young Yehiel Michel's later understanding of worldly affairs, economics, and monetary laws.[2]

Rabbi Epstein's Torah education was shaped under the guidance of Rabbi Eliyahu Goldberg, head of the rabbinical court of Bobruisk, who was his primary teacher.[1, 2] Already in his youth he was notable for exceptional talents and an inclination toward order and clarity of thought. In 1865 he was appointed rabbi in the town of Novozybkov, a community characterized by a predominantly Hasidic population. Rabbi Epstein, despite being Lithuanian in origin and training, integrated well into this community. Scholars such as Itam Henkin note that it is possible that many of his early compositions were influenced by the need to make halakhah accessible to an audience of Hasidic character, as well as by the need to ensure the distribution of his books among this diverse public.[2]

In 1883 Rabbi Epstein moved to Navahrudak (Novogrudok), where he served as town rabbi for approximately 24 years until his death on March 24, 1908 (22 Adar II 5668).[1, 2] His tenure in Navahrudak was the peak period of his halakhic creativity. As an active pulpit rabbi, he dealt daily with practical questions, neighborly disputes, and communal problems, which gave his adjudication its realistic character, connected to reality, in contrast to theoretical adjudication detached from practical life.[3, 4]

The Torah and Family Network: A Dynasty of Influence

Rabbi Epstein's family was a "choir" of Torah and communal talents, each of whom contributed in his own way to the Jewish world and left an indelible mark. The family connections that Rabbi Epstein wove were not merely a private matter, but rather an extensive Torah network that linked different centers of Torah study in Eastern Europe.[1, 2]

His son, Rabbi Barukh Halevi Epstein, became famous as the author of the commentary "Torah Temimah" ("Perfect Torah") on the Pentateuch, a work that integrates halakhah and aggadah according to the order of biblical verses in an innovative manner.[1, 2] His second son, Rabbi Dov Ber Epstein, was among the activists of the Old Yishuv in Jerusalem and served as a connecting link between diaspora Jewry and the developing community in the Land of Israel.[1, 2] His daughter, Batya Miriam, was married in a second marriage to Rabbi Epstein's brother-in-law, the Netziv of Volozhin, head of the legendary Volozhin yeshiva.[1, 2] This connection linked the communal rabbinate in Navahrudak with the Lithuanian yeshiva world at its peak. His grandson, the son of Batya Miriam, was Rabbi Meir Bar-Ilan, among the leaders of religious Zionism and founder of the Encyclopaedia Talmudica, who translated his grandfather's halakhic heritage into the language of modern national action.[1, 5]

Rabbi Epstein's daughter, Breina Volbrinsky (Warhaftig-Shachor), played a critical role in the continuity of her father's enterprise when she served as the printer of the "Arukh HaShulhan" volumes, a fact attesting to active and exceptional female involvement in managing the family Torah enterprise.[1, 2] Rabbi Meir Bar-Ilan describes in his memoirs how his grandfather would write his books while conducting rabbinical court sessions, a fact attesting to phenomenal powers of concentration and to the fact that writing was an integral part of his dynamic activity as communal rabbi and head of the rabbinical court.[5]

Halakhic Methodology: The Structure and Style of the "Arukh HaShulhan"

Rabbi Epstein's central work, the "Arukh HaShulhan," is a life's work unprecedented in its scope. In contrast to many other compositions that focused on specific parts of the Shulhan Arukh relating to daily life, Rabbi Epstein aspired to encompass all of the Torah. The book was written on all four parts of the Shulhan Arukh: Orah Hayyim, Yoreh De'ah, Even HaEzer, and Hoshen Mishpat.[5, 6]

Rabbi Epstein's methodology in clarifying the law is systematic and didactic, and its purpose is to show the evolution of halakhah from its original source to its practical application in his day. Each section in the "Arukh HaShulhan" is not merely a commentary on the text, but rather an independent essay organized in the following manner [3, 4, 7]:

Talmudic sources: The discussion always begins with clarification of the sugya in the Babylonian Talmud, and often in the Jerusalem Talmud as well, to which Rabbi Epstein gave particularly great weight.[3, 5]

Approaches of the Rishonim: In-depth analysis of the approaches of Rashi, Tosafot, the Rif, the Rosh, and the Rambam. The emphasis on the Rambam's approach is especially prominent in his work.[3, 7]

Adjudication of the Shulhan Arukh and the Rema: Presentation of the ruling of the Mehaber (Rabbi Joseph Karo) and the glosses of the Rema that constitute the foundation for Ashkenazic adjudication.[7, 8]

Analysis of the Aharonim: Review and discussion of the words of the great Aharonim such as the Magen Avraham, the Taz, the Shakh, and the Noda BiYehudah, while resolving contradictions and bringing original novellae.[7, 9]

Adjudication and justification of custom: Summary of the practical halakhah, with a pronounced tendency to justify the accepted Jewish custom.[5]

The language of the book is described as "clear and easy language," which enables even one who is not an outstanding Torah scholar to follow the evolution of the law and understand its reasoning.[5, 10] The goal was to convey the "bottom line" with maximum clarity, while skipping unnecessary pilpul that does not contribute to practical adjudication.[11]

The Status of Custom: "Jewish Custom Is Torah" as a Principle of Adjudication

One of the most pronounced characteristics of the "Arukh HaShulhan" is its respectful and grounding relationship to Jewish custom. For Rabbi Epstein, the custom prevalent in Jewish communities is not merely a folkloristic matter, but rather an expression of "To
alive." He tended to believe that the people of Israel, guided by its sages throughout the generations, does not err in its established customs.[5]

In cases where an apparent contradiction was found between the words of early halakhic authorities and the accepted custom, Rabbi Epstein labored to find halakhic support for the custom and to reconcile it with the sources. This approach granted the book great popularity among community rabbis, who found in it backing for the reality of life in their communities and for their personal authority as rabbis.[2, 4] A striking example of this can be found in his discussions of the customs regarding haircuts and marriages during the counting of the Omer, where he analyzes the various customs and justifies the local custom ("our custom") against other approaches.[12]

Phenomenological Comparison: "Arukh HaShulhan" versus the "Mishnah Berurah"

The discussion of Rabbi Epstein's character is incomplete without comparison to his principal halakhic counterpart—the book "Mishnah Berurah" by Rabbi Yisrael Meir HaKohen of Radin (the "Hafetz Hayyim").[3, 4, 5] The two books were published almost simultaneously and became the two pillars of Ashkenazic halakhic decision-making, yet they represent entirely different approaches.

The "Mishnah Berurah" is perceived as the classic yeshiva textbook, presenting the range of halakhic possibilities while preferring stringency as a more "secure" path religiously. In contrast, the "Arukh HaShulhan" is the book of the practical decisor, one who must give a decisive and conclusive answer.[3] Rabbi Yosef Eliyahu Henkin preferred the "Arukh HaShulhan" because the author saw the words of the "Mishnah Berurah" (in the sections that were published) and nevertheless chose at times to rule differently, which grants him the status of "batra'i" (a later decisor who was familiar with his predecessor's words and deliberated on them).[3, 5]

"Arukh HaShulhan HaAtid": The Redemptive Vision and Comprehensive Codification

An exceptional expression of Rabbi Epstein's Torah aspirations is his work "Arukh HaShulhan HaAtid." While most halakhic authorities focused only on the laws practiced at present, Rabbi Epstein chose to write a complete halakhic code on all those laws that have not been practiced since the destruction of the Temple.[5, 10] In this he resembled Maimonides, who was the only one before him who sought to encompass all the Torah in practical and systematic decision-making.[5, 14]

The book is divided into four major areas, covering the entire world of commandments not currently practiced [10]:

Zera'im: Laws dependent on the Land including pe'ah, shevi'it, yovel, terumot and ma'asrot, and the laws of demai and bikkurim.[10]

Qodashim: Laws of the chosen house, the Temple vessels, the sacrificial service, the daily and additional offerings, and the Yom Kippur service.[10]

Toharot: A complex system of laws of corpse impurity, the red heifer, negaim, and the laws of impurity of foods and vessels.[10]

Liqutim: Laws of Naziriteship, valuations and dedications, the Sanhedrin, rebellious authorities, kings, and shekels.[10]

The writing of these laws reflects a consciousness of active anticipation of redemption and faith that the Torah world must be legally prepared for implementation of the Torah in its entirety with the renewal of Jewish national existence in the Land of Israel.[14] His grandson, Rabbi Meir Bar-Ilan, was the driving force behind the printing of these sections, thereby connecting the grandfather's halakhic enterprise with the national enterprise of Religious Zionism.[5, 13]

"The Boldness of a Decisor": Social Thought and a View toward Modernity

Modern academic research, and especially the work of Professor Simcha Fishbane, emphasizes Rabbi Epstein's "boldness" within the conservative halakhic world.[4, 15, 16] This boldness was expressed not only in his willingness to disagree with great Aharonim, but also in his complex and relatively open attitude toward the social and technological changes of his era.

General Education and Attitude toward Science

In his sermons collected in the book "Qol Ben Levi," Rabbi Epstein presents an original position regarding general studies. He viewed secular wisdom as a "complement" to religious studies.[4] According to his approach, general education can assist in understanding the Torah and the proper functioning of the rabbi and leader within modern society.[16] This approach was different from the extreme separatism that characterized other parts of Lithuanian Jewry, and it reflects his understanding that traditional Judaism must know how to contend with the challenges of the times and not merely fortify itself behind walls.[4]

Politics and Social Stability: "Kavod Melekh"

In his introduction to the Hoshen Mishpat section, Rabbi Epstein included an essay entitled "Kavod Melekh," in which he expresses loyalty to the Russian Tsarist regime.[9, 17] To be sure, this can be seen as an apologetic step intended to protect the community from censorship, but Fishbane argues that it also reflects a halakhic conception that recognizes the importance of governmental stability in preventing anarchy ("were it not for the fear of the kingdom").[4, 18] For him, the preservation of social order is a necessary condition for the existence of the Torah legal system.[4]

Women and Their Status in the Halakhic Sphere

Rabbi Epstein displayed sensitivity and awareness regarding the status of women in Jewish society. In the "Arukh HaShulhan" he discusses their obligations and rights, providing a lenient interpretation in places where this was possible within the framework of halakhah, from an understanding of their central role in preserving the Jewish home and tradition.[4, 16] For example, in the laws of labor during the counting of the Omer or in mourning customs, he reveals consideration for the practical reality of their lives.[12]

Halakhic Decision-Making as Example: Between Theory and Practice

To understand the force of his decision-making, one may examine two areas in which he left his unique imprint: the writing of Torah scrolls and the laws of the days of counting the Omer.

Writing a Torah Scroll and Making Torah Accessible

In his discussions of the commandment to write a Torah scroll, Rabbi Epstein brings the position of the Rosh and the Tur, according to which in our time the essence of the commandment is to write (or purchase) Humashim, Mishnayot, and Talmudic volumes with their commentaries, so that one can study from them.[19] He emphasizes that the original purpose of writing a Torah scroll was personal study ("and teach it to the children of Israel, place it in their mouths"), and since today Torah scrolls in the synagogue are designated only for public reading, a person must invest his resources in accessible study texts.[19] This approach reflects his dynamic conception: halakhah must adapt the means of the commandment to its essential purpose within a changing historical context.

Mourning Customs During the Counting of the Omer

Rabbi Epstein analyzes in detail the various customs concerning haircuts and marriages during the days of counting the Omer. He notes the custom of the "Beit Yosef" to wait until the morning of the thirty-fourth day, as opposed to the prevalent Ashkenazic custom to be lenient on Lag BaOmer.[12] He emphasizes the prohibition of "lo titgodedu"—the importance of maintaining uniform custom within the same city, in order to prevent disputes and division within the community.[12]

Reception and Influence: The Transformations of a Decisor in the Mirror of the Generations

The process of reception of the "Arukh HaShulhan" underwent dramatic vicissitudes throughout the twentieth and twenty-first centuries, reflecting the shifts in the centers of gravity of the Torah world.

Until the Holocaust: The book was very popular in Ashkenazic and Eastern European communities. It was printed many times and was considered the principal practical halakhic work for community rabbis because of its scope and clarity.[5, 13]

After the Holocaust and the Growth of the Yeshiva World in Israel: The influence of the Hazon Ish, who determined that the "Mishnah Berurah" is the decisive authority for the Lithuanian public, led to the marginalization of the "Arukh HaShulhan" from the central yeshiva world.[5] Many customs based on the "Arukh HaShulhan" were abandoned in favor of the rulings of the "Mishnah Berurah."[5]

Influence in the United States: In the Orthodox community in the U.S., the book's status was preserved to a much greater extent, through the influence of decisors such as Rabbi Moshe Feinstein and Rabbi Joseph B. Soloveitchik, who appreciated Rabbi Epstein's realistic judgment.[3, 5]

The Modern Renaissance: In recent years a return to the use of the "Arukh HaShulhan" is evident even in Israel. The publication of new editions, its incorporation in rabbinic examinations, and renewed academic and rabbinic interest in his method attest to the recognition of the vitality of a decisor who combines profound learning with broad social understanding.[13, 14]

Additional Works and His Literary Œuvre

In addition to "Aru
Beyond the Arukh HaShulḥan ("The Set Table"), Rabbi Epstein left an extensive literary legacy demonstrating the breadth of his intellectual horizons:

Or LaYesharim ("Light for the Upright"): A commentary on Sefer HaYashar ("The Book of the Upright"), attributed to Rabbeinu Tam, exemplifying his capacity to engage with complex moral and scholarly issues.[1, 10]

Mikhal HaMayim ("Vessel of Water"): A commentary on the Palestinian Talmud, expressing his profound appreciation for the Land of Israel tradition as a complementary foundation to the Babylonian [Talmud].[1, 3]

Leil Shimurim ("Night of Vigil"): A commentary on the Passover Haggadah, combining theological concepts with halakhic explanations of the festival's customs.[1, 2]

Kol Ben Levi ("Voice of the Son of Levi"): A collection of his sermons, providing a window into his worldview regarding leadership, education, and relations with general society.[4]

Summary and Conclusions

Rabbi Yeḥiel Mikhel HaLevi Epstein was far more than a halakhic decisor; he was an architect of a comprehensive Jewish legal system that sought to encompass past, present, and future. In the Arukh HaShulḥan, he created a work that integrates the profound Lithuanian scholarship with the social sensitivity of a communal rabbi familiar with the daily hardships of his flock.[3, 5]

His halakhic boldness, manifested in his defense of Jewish customs, his openness to modernity, and his composition of laws for the future, establishes him as a central figure bridging the world of traditional heritage and the challenges facing the Jewish people in the modern era.[4, 10, 14] Although he suffered a certain marginalization in favor of the Mishnah Berurah during the twentieth century, his teaching is today returning to center stage in the halakhic arena, offering a model of connected, balanced, and courageous jurisprudence that serves as an inspiration for generations of decisors and scholars.[5] The scope of his work, from the depths of Talmudic foundations to the forefront of practical halakhic decision-making, ensures that the voice of the rabbi of Novogrudok will continue to resonate in the halls of Torah and Jewish life for many years to come.[1, 2]
